newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Low inputs take toll on Sao Paulo orange crop.
newsitem.headline: Low inputs take toll on Sao Paulo orange crop.

text.p: Despite optimal weather and smooth overall harvesting conditions, industry sources still expect a lower Sao Paulo orange crop in 1996/97 as financial problems have prompted a decline in grove care.
Farmers have cut their use of insecticides and fertilisers as a result of lower prices and a lack of available credit, analysts said.

"We have had very bad prices so that most growers couldn't buy fertilisers," said Leonardo Kossoy, president of the Association of Citrus Growers of Sao Paulo State (Aciesp). "Not only that, we have had a lot of typical orange diseases."
These included the yellow CVC virus, which affected mainly young trees and for which no effective treatment had yet been found, Kossoy said.

Brazil's Association of Citrus Exporters (Abecitrus) is due to publish its final estimate for the 1996/97 Sao Paulo harvest by the end of December but said it would be little changed from the 352 million boxes it forecast in May.
This compares with 357 million boxes in the 1995/96 marketing year.
"If there is any change it won't be a very big one," said Abecitrus president Adermeval Garcia, adding that the first crop estimate for 1997/98 would be released in May.
"The weather has been marvellous," Garcia said. "It's been a very normal year, we didn't have any kind of surprises."

The May Abecitrus estimate is in line with a November report from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) attache in Brazil, which revised downwards its previous forecast of Sao Paulo 1996/1997 production by 0.5 percent to 353 million boxes.
Brazil's orange crop was expected to total 401 million boxes, down 0.5 percent on the previous forecast and down from 405 million in the previous year, the USDA report said.
But Aciesp's Kossoy said he thought those figure were optimistic. "I think Brazilian production isn't growing as much as they say," he said, declining however to offer an alternative figure.
"I think production will be lower and will remain similar next year," Kossoy said. "After next year production will start to decline."
Kossoy said a lot of new plants had come into production this year, but they were only yielding 10 to 20 kilos compared with 60 to 80 kilos from more mature trees.

He predicted planting would sharply decline and added that a spectacular rise in domestic consumption of orange juice in recent years, although it provided the market with some support, was not sufficient to push prices higher.
